subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the determinant with rows (a²+2a, 2a+1, 1), (2a+1, a+2, 1) and (3, 3, 1) is equal to (a − 1)³.

mark_split.label: Row operations R₁ → R₁ − R₂ and R₂ → R₂ − R₃
Take (a − 1) common from R₁ and from R₂

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.49, chapter 5 MATRICES, Long Answer question 8, determinant-identity route. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 3+2+2+1 split gives three marks to the pair of row subtractions, because they are the whole idea and the longest arithmetic, two to the common factors, two to the expansion and one to the stated result. The opening line carries no mark because it only copies the question down. Working checked: the identity was tested on a = 2, where the determinant of (8, 5, 1), (5, 4, 1), (3, 3, 1) is 1 = (2 − 1)³, and on a = 3, where the determinant of (15, 7, 1), (7, 5, 1), (3, 3, 1) is 8 = (3 − 1)³. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2; Matrices is one of the units that can fill a Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say which rows you subtract, what comes out common, which line you expand along, and how the cube appears.

steps.label: Write the determinant
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Look at column 3 first: it is 1, 1, 1. Subtracting neighbouring rows turns two of those 1s into 0s, and a column of 0, 0, 1 makes the expansion at the end almost free.
steps.memory_tip: Column 3 is 1, 1, 1. Subtracting neighbouring rows turns two of those 1s into zeros.
lines: Column 3 is 1, 1, 1, so subtracting one row
from the next will clear two of those 1s.

recall.must_convey: That the working starts from the given determinant, with column 3 noted as 1, 1, 1. Naming the move is full credit.

take delta as the determinant in the question

write down the determinant that has to be proved

steps.why: The answer is a cube of (a − 1) while no single entry contains (a − 1). That mismatch always means something has to be subtracted first.
common_mistakes: Expanding directly, which produces a page of terms in a.
Missing that column 3 is 1, 1, 1, and hunting for a common factor instead.

steps.label: Subtract neighbouring rows
steps.margin_note: Three marks, and the whole idea. Both subtractions use the row BELOW, and row 3 is left untouched. Subtracting one row from another never changes a determinant, so no factor appears or disappears here.
steps.memory_tip: Both subtractions use the row BELOW, and row 3 is left untouched.
lines: R₁ → R₁ − R₂,  R₂ → R₂ − R₃

recall.must_convey: That R₁ − R₂ and R₂ − R₃ are applied, clearing the top two entries of column 3 and leaving a² − 1, a − 1 and 2a − 2, a − 1.
accept: subtract row two from row one and row three from row two so the last column becomes zero zero one
apply R one minus R two and R two minus R three leaving a squared minus one and a minus one
take the differences of neighbouring rows to clear the third column
R1 minus R2, R2 minus R3 cheste last column lo rendu zeros vastai
subtract the row below from each of the first two rows
reject: apply R one minus R two

steps.why: Subtracting one row from another leaves a determinant unchanged. It earns its place here because the +2a and the +1s cancel, turning quadratics into products that carry a factor of (a − 1).
common_mistakes: Writing R₁ → R₂ − R₁ instead of R₁ → R₁ − R₂, which flips the sign of the determinant.
Changing row 3 as well, so there is no row of plain numbers left.
Working out a²+2a − (2a+1) as a²+1 by dropping the bracket.

steps.label: Take (a − 1) common
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Row 1 gives (a−1) through the difference of two squares; row 2 gives it by taking 2 out as well. Two rows, two factors — that is (a−1)², and the third factor comes later.
steps.memory_tip: Row 1 gives (a−1) from a² − 1; row 2 gives it from 2a − 2. Two rows, two factors.
lines: so (a−1) comes out of R₁ and out of R₂:

recall.must_convey: That (a−1) is a factor of both a² − 1 and 2a − 2, so it comes out of rows 1 and 2, giving (a−1)² outside.
accept: a squared minus one is a minus one into a plus one and two a minus two is two into a minus one so a minus one comes out of both rows
take a minus one common from the first two rows giving a minus one squared outside
both rows carry a factor of a minus one so it comes out twice
rendu rows lo a minus one common undi, so a minus one square bayata vasthundi
pull a minus one out of row one and row two

steps.why: A common factor of a whole row comes outside the determinant. Two of the three factors of the answer are collected here, which is why the remaining 2×2 work only has to produce one more.
common_mistakes: Taking 2(a−1) out of R₂ and still writing that row as 1, 1, 0; only (a−1) comes out, so the row is 2, 1, 0.
Forgetting that the second entry a − 1 also has to be divided, leaving a − 1 inside.
Taking the factor out of a column instead of a row.

steps.label: Expand along C₃
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Expand along the column with two zeros, never along a full row. The surviving 2×2 is the top-left block, and its sign is plus because the 1 sits in position (3, 3).
steps.memory_tip: Expand along the column with two zeros. The surviving 2×2 is the top-left block, sign plus.
lines: Column 3 is 0, 0, 1, so only the bottom entry
contributes. Its cofactor sign is plus:

recall.must_convey: That expanding along column 3 leaves one term, (a+1)(1) − 1(2) = a − 1, multiplied by the (a−1)² outside.
accept: expand along the third column so only one term survives and the two by two gives a plus one minus two
the last column is zero zero one so one term is left and it comes to a minus one
expand down column three and the minor is a plus one minus two which is a minus one
third column lo rendu zeros unnai kabatti oke term migulutundi
only the bottom entry contributes and its minor gives a minus one

steps.why: Expanding along a line of zeros removes two of the three terms before any arithmetic is done. Choosing that line is the difference between three 2×2 determinants and one.
common_mistakes: Expanding along the first row, which needs three 2×2 determinants.
Giving the surviving term a minus sign; position (3, 3) is plus.

steps.label: State the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Count where each (a−1) came from: one from row 1, one from row 2, one from the 2×2. If you can only account for two, a factor was dropped in the common-factor step.
steps.memory_tip: Count where each (a−1) came from: row 1, row 2, and the 2×2. Three in all.
lines: Two factors came out of the rows and one came
from the 2×2 determinant — three in all:

recall.must_convey: That the three factors of (a−1) multiply to (a−1)³, which is the required right-hand side.
accept: three factors of a minus one give a minus one cubed
two from the rows and one from the two by two make the cube
the answer is a minus one whole cubed
moodu factors kalipithe a minus one cube avthundi
multiply them to get a minus one cube which is the RHS

steps.why: Counting the factors is the check. The answer is a cube, so exactly three of them must be accounted for, and no numerical factor such as 2 may be left over.
common_mistakes: Writing (a−1)² by forgetting one of the row factors.
Leaving a stray 2 in front from the 2a − 2 row.
